youtube.title: The Lift Button That Was Never Connected #Shorts
youtube.description:
Ava is late for the most important interview of her life. She hits the close button. Again. And again.

In many lifts, that button does nothing. In the US, the 1990 disability law (the ADA) means doors must stay open long enough for someone on crutches or in a wheelchair, so in many lifts the close-door button was simply switched off in normal use - it only works for firefighters in key-operated fire service mode. And it's not just lifts: in 2004, New York City figures showed more than 2,500 of its 3,250 crosswalk buttons did nothing. Why keep them? Pressing a button feels like control - psychologists call it the illusion of control.

How many times have you pressed it today?

Sources:
- 'Door close' buttons on most elevators don't actually work (CBS, citing the NYT and the National Elevator Industry): https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/door-close-elevator-button-dont-work-placebo
- Firefighters' Phase II operation and the door-close button (IUEC code alert, ASME A17.1): https://iuec.org/wp-content/uploads/IUEC-Codes-Standards-Alert-Phase-II-Operation-1-1.pdf
- NYC crosswalk buttons, 2004 figures: https://designobserver.com/information-design-and-the-placebo-effect
- Langer (1975), The illusion of control, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 32(2)

Ava and the interview are fictional. Lift buttons vary by building and country.
